1: \section{From frozen confidence to current-curvature scores}\label{sec:abstract-transport}
2: 
3: Consider a learner choosing from a finite list of available actions $\cA_t$
4: at round $t$.  After observing the context, it forms a prediction of each
5: action's true mean reward $\mu_t^*(a)$ and chooses an action $a_t$ whose reward could plausibly
6: be high.  Only the chosen reward is then revealed.
7: An \emph{upper confidence bound} (UCB) makes this rule precise: its score adds
8: an uncertainty allowance to a prediction.  We call the score \emph{optimistic}
9: when it upper-bounds the true mean reward of every available action on the
10: stated confidence and certificate event.  This is a claim about mean rewards,
11: not about every noisy reward that the learner might observe.
12: 
13: \paragraph{What changes when the model is retrained?}
14: The feature vector used to interpret a past reward was fixed before that
15: reward arrived.  Keeping these collection-time vectors gives a frozen
16: reference matrix with the sequential update used by the confidence argument.
17: Recomputing the past vectors at the current model can give a different matrix,
18: even though no new rewards have been collected.  The question is how to use
19: this current matrix without silently assuming that the original confidence
20: argument still applies.
21: 
22: The prediction query $\bq_t(a)$ is the vector whose uncertainty matters for
23: action $a$; in the nonlinear specialization it is the current prediction
24: gradient.  A metric here is a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix: its
25: quadratic form is positive in every nonzero direction.  A query's \emph{width}
26: is its norm under the inverse metric.  It measures a geometric scale, not a
27: confidence level by itself.  Statistical confidence also needs a valid
28: nonnegative radius $\beta_t$, a prediction center $m_t(a)$, and a nonnegative
29: error allowance $b_t(a)$.  A smaller width after retraining therefore does not, by itself,
30: show that prediction error has become smaller.  A \emph{certificate} is a
31: bound that guarantees a required comparison or numerical property; measuring
32: a small discrepancy in an experiment is not itself such a guarantee.
33: 
34: \paragraph{Start with an exact current matrix and exact widths.}
35: For the moment, suppose the learner computes the current matrix and its
36: width $s_t(a)$ exactly.  Suppose also that a statistical argument bounds the
37: absolute prediction error by $\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a)$ in the frozen matrix.
38: A \emph{path certificate} bounds change along an auxiliary matrix path joining
39: the frozen and current matrices; this need not be the learner's training
40: trajectory.  A valid certificate $\bar D_t$ supplies the comparison
41: $\bar s_t(a)\le e^{\bar D_t/2}s_t(a)$ for every action.  Thus the exact-case
42: score is
43: \[
44:  U_t(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t e^{\bar D_t/2}s_t(a)+b_t(a).
45: \]
46: On the joint confidence and certificate event, this score upper-bounds the
47: mean reward.  The multiplier enlarges the current width enough to retain
48: the supplied reference confidence.  The center must be the one justified by
49: that confidence argument; it need not be the raw nonlinear prediction.
50: \Cref{sec:corrected-center} shows how to construct it.
51: 
52: This exact case explains what transport provides: a justification for a score
53: built around current curvature.  Direct reference scoring remains an
54: alternative.  The transport argument alone establishes neither a smaller
55: uncertainty allowance nor better action choices.  The general result next
56: also allows an approximate matrix, numerical width computation, and an
57: approximately maximizing action selector.
58: 
59: \paragraph{How to read the argument.}
60: We first assume a confidence band in the frozen metric and state the
61: conditions that let a current-metric score use it.  The main result is
62: \Cref{thm:transported-ucb}; its interpretation follows the statement.
63: \Cref{sec:logarithmic-transport} then supplies geometric comparisons between
64: metrics, and \Cref{sec:corrected-center} constructs the confidence band for
65: squared loss.  \Cref{sec:closed-rates-new} combines these pieces into regret
66: rates and explains the sharper comparison available for scaled tanh.
67: The finite-action picture above is enough to follow these constructions;
68: the general protocol below also covers action spaces that cannot be listed.
69: 
70: \paragraph{The matrices and their widths.}
71: Let $\bq_t(a)\in\R^d$ be the prediction query.  We distinguish the frozen
72: reference matrix $\bVbar_t$, the exact current matrix $\bV_t$, and the SPD
73: matrix $\Calg_t$ that the algorithm actually applies.  They are also called
74: metrics because they define the norms used for uncertainty.  The reference
75: matrix has the following update, whereas the current and applied matrices
76: need not have a rank-one update:
77: \begin{align}
78:  \bVbar_1&=\lambda\bI,\nonumber\\
79:  \bVbar_{t+1}&=\bVbar_t+\sigma^{-2}\bq_t(a_t)\bq_t(a_t)^\top,
80:  \label{eq:reference-update-new}\\
81:  \bV_t&=\text{the exact current relinearized metric},\nonumber\\
82:  \Calg_t&=\text{the algorithmic SPD metric}.
83: \end{align}
84: Here $\lambda>0$ is the ridge regularization and $\sigma>0$ sets the scale
85: of the updates; it is the noise scale in the squared-loss specialization.
86: The reference update keeps each query as it was at collection time.
87: For the same current query, the matrices can give different widths:
88: \begin{equation}\label{eq:three-widths-new}
89:  \begin{aligned}
90:   \bar s_t^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\bVbar_t^{-1}\bq_t(a),\\
91:   s_t^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\bV_t^{-1}\bq_t(a),\\
92:   s_{\Calg,t}^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\Calg_t^{-1}\bq_t(a).
93:  \end{aligned}
94: \end{equation}
95: These are exact mathematical widths.  The computed upper width
96: $\hat s_t(a)$ will be a separate object, because a numerical solver need not
97: return the exact width of $\Calg_t$.
98: \Cref{tab:transport-notation} collects these distinctions and the score terms
99: introduced below.  Their precise requirements remain in
100: \Cref{asm:abstract-transport} and the score-selection condition.
101:

103: \caption{Notation for confidence transport.  Widths are geometric scales;
104: the confidence and certificate assumptions justify their use in a score.}
105: \label{tab:transport-notation}

107: \begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}p{.22\columnwidth}X@{}}
108: \toprule
109: Symbol & Meaning \\
110: \midrule

131: The frozen update also gives a way to control widths accumulated over time.
132: Its log-determinant growth, called the \emph{frozen information gain}, is
133: \begin{equation}\label{eq:frozen-gamma-new}
134:  \gamma_T
135:  :=\log\frac{\det\bVbar_{T+1}}{\det\bVbar_1}
136:  =\sum_{t=1}^T\log\!\left(1+\sigma^{-2}\bar s_t^2(a_t)\right).
137: \end{equation}
138: Each term records the contribution of the action actually chosen.  This
139: identity is why the regret proof returns to the frozen matrix even when the
140: policy scores actions using the current matrix.  Set $\gamma_0=0$, and define
141: regret as the mean reward lost relative to the best available action:
142: \begin{equation}\label{eq:regret-definition-new}
143:  \operatorname{reg}_t
144:  :=\sup_{a\in\cA_t}\mu_t^*(a)-\mu_t^*(a_t),
145:  \qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\operatorname{reg}_t.
146: \end{equation}
147: Throughout the theory, ``regret'' means this sum of mean-reward gaps, also
148: called \emph{cumulative pseudo-regret}.  The selected history can be random,
149: but the summands compare mean rewards rather than realized noisy rewards.
150: 
151: \paragraph{Read the protocol in chronological order.}
152: First observe the context and available actions.  The prefix history then
153: determines the reference and current matrices before this round's fresh
154: algorithmic randomness.  Next, use any permitted pre-reward randomness to construct the
155: operator, certificates, and scores and select an action.  Only after selection
156: is its reward observed and the statistics updated.  We call quantities fixed
157: before the fresh randomness \emph{predictable}; \emph{pre-reward measurable}
158: quantities may use that randomness but cannot use the new reward.
159: 
160: For measurably enumerated finite action lists,
161: \Cref{cor:finite-enumeration-new} reduces the general action-space selection
162: and measurability details to finite maxima and intersections.  Readers working
163: in that setting can skim those details in the next paragraph.  The timing,
164: reference-confidence, and matrix and solver certificate requirements still
165: apply; finite enumeration does not supply them.
166: 
167: \paragraph{General protocol and timing.}
168: Let $(\mathsf A,\mathcal B)$ be a standard Borel action space.  At round $t$,
169: the learner observes a context and a nonempty random action correspondence
170: $\cA_t:\Omega\to 2^{\mathsf A}$ whose graph
171: \[
172:  \operatorname{Gr}(\cA_t)
173:  :=\{(\omega,a):a\in\cA_t(\omega)\}
174:  \in\cHist_t^-\otimes\mathcal B.
175: \]
176: Here $\cHist_t^-$ is the history after the context and action correspondence
177: are observed but before fresh round-$t$ algorithmic randomization.  The variable
178: $\Omega_t$ records all round-$t$ pre-reward randomization, which may be revealed
179: in sequential stages, and $\cHist_t=\cHist_t^-\vee\sigma(\Omega_t)$ contains
180: that randomization but not the reward.  The restrictions to
181: $\operatorname{Gr}(\cA_t)$ of
182: $(\omega,a)\mapsto\mu_t^*(a),\bq_t(a),m_t(a),b_t(a),\hat s_t(a)$, and, once
183: defined below, $U_t(a)$ are assumed jointly measurable with respect to
184: $\cHist_t\otimes\mathcal B$.  We also assume explicitly that
185: $\sup_{a\in\cA_t}\mu_t^*(a)$ and $\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t(a)$ are finite
186: $\cHist_t$-measurable random variables, that the oracle below returns a $\cHist_t$-measurable
187: selector in $\cA_t$, and that the simultaneous confidence and all certificate
188: events below, including path, operator, all-domain solver-upper, and
189: played-action sharpness validity, are measurable.  These are
190: substantive assumptions; standard-Borel structure
191: and graph measurability alone do not make every supremum or selector measurable.
192: 
193: The reference metric $\bVbar_t$ and, when used, the representation parameter
194: $\btheta_t$ are determined from the prefix history and are
195: $\cHist_t^-$-measurable.  The exact current metric $\bV_t$ is likewise formed
196: before the fresh certificate randomization and is $\cHist_t^-$-measurable.  The realized algorithmic operator
197: $\Calg_t$, path envelope $\bar D_t$, condition factors
198: $\kappa_{-,t},\kappa_{+,t}$, solver-width map $\hat s_t(\cdot)$, sharpness
199: factor $\alpha_t$, oracle tolerance $\xi_t$, and selected action $a_t$ may
200: depend on $\Omega_t$ and are required only to be $\cHist_t$-measurable.  Thus
201: ``predictable'' below is reserved for $\cHist_t^-$-measurable quantities;
202: quantities that may use $\Omega_t$ are called pre-reward measurable.  The
203: reward is observed only after $a_t$ is selected.
204: 
205: \paragraph{What must be certified.}
206: The next assumption separates statistical confidence from the comparisons
207: needed to use it.  The confidence band concerns the center $m_t(a)$ and the
208: frozen width.  The path and operator certificates compare matrices.  The
209: solver certificate controls the width that enters the score.
210: Its quantifiers have different jobs: an upper-valid width is needed for every
211: scored action to preserve optimism, while an upper bound on excess width
212: (``sharpness'') is needed only for the action played to control regret.
213: All of these objects must be available before that action's reward is seen.
214: 
215: \begin{assumption}[Reference confidence and operational certificates]
216: \label{asm:abstract-transport}
217: For predictable $\beta_t\ge0$ and pre-reward measurable center $m_t(a)$ and
218: action-dependent envelope $b_t(a)\ge0$, a measurable simultaneous confidence
219: event satisfies
220: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-confidence-new}
221:  |\mu_t^*(a)-m_t(a)|\le\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a)
222:  \qquad\text{for every }a\in\cA_t.
223: \end{equation}
224: There is an absolutely continuous SPD path $\bV_t(\tau)$ from
225: $\bVbar_t$ to $\bV_t$ with a pre-reward certificate
226: \begin{equation}\label{eq:path-length-new}
227:  \begin{aligned}
228:   \mathcal D_t
229:   &:=\int_0^1\!\left\|
230:   \bV_t(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV_t(\tau)\bV_t(\tau)^{-1/2}
231:   \right\|_{\rm op}d\tau\\
232:   &\le\bar D_t<\infty.
233:  \end{aligned}
234: \end{equation}
235: The algorithmic operator has a pre-reward two-sided certificate
236: \begin{equation}\label{eq:operator-sandwich-new}
237:  0<\kappa_{-,t}\le\kappa_{+,t}<\infty,\qquad
238:  \kappa_{-,t}\bV_t\preceq\Calg_t\preceq\kappa_{+,t}\bV_t.
239: \end{equation}
240: Finally, the solver returns a jointly measurable pre-reward width map
241: $\hat s_t(a)\ge0$ such that, on a measurable solver event,
242: \begin{equation}\label{eq:solver-interface-new}
243:  \begin{aligned}
244:   s_{\Calg,t}(a)&\le\hat s_t(a)
245:   &&\text{for every }a\in\cA_t,\\
246:   \hat s_t(a_t)&\le\alpha_t s_{\Calg,t}(a_t),
247:   &&\alpha_t\ge1.
248:  \end{aligned}
249: \end{equation}
250: The first condition is an all-domain optimism certificate.  The second is
251: required only at the played action.
252: \end{assumption}
253: 
254: The general score combines the center, the converted uncertainty allowance,
255: and the current error allowance.  The operator factor accounts for using
256: $\Calg_t$ in place of $\bV_t$, and $\hat s_t(a)$ is the width actually used
257: by the selector:
258: \begin{equation}\label{eq:transported-score-new}
259:  U_t(a)=m_t(a)
260:  +\beta_t e^{\bar D_t/2}\sqrt{\kappa_{+,t}}\,\hat s_t(a)
261:  +b_t(a),
262: \end{equation}
263: Let a pre-reward oracle return a $\cHist_t$-measurable selector
264: $a_t\in\cA_t$ satisfying
265: \begin{equation}\label{eq:approx-score-oracle-new}
266:  U_t(a_t)\ge\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t(a)-\xi_t,\qquad \xi_t\ge0.
267: \end{equation}
268: The tolerance $\xi_t$ measures how far the selected score may fall below the
269: best score; it is not a condition on nonlinear model training.  Regret is
270: defined against the mean-reward supremum, so an optimal action need not exist.
271: 
272: \begin{remark}[One realized solver-width map]
273: The all-domain solver upper condition, the played-action sharpness condition,
274: and the approximate-score-oracle inequality refer to the same realized width
275: map $\hat s_t(\cdot)$.  Refining the selected action's solve after selection
276: must not silently replace the value used in $U_t(a_t)$.  If refinement changes
277: $\hat s_t(a_t)$, the oracle inequality must be checked again, or the original
278: score width must remain the theorem object.  Any randomized post-selection
279: verification needs its own pre-draw filtration and conditional failure
280: allocation.  No all-action sharpness condition is required.
281: \end{remark}

305: \paragraph{The regret guarantee.}
306: Under these conditions, optimism bounds the loss at the selected action by
307: its uncertainty and bias terms.  Comparing that selected width back to the
308: reference width lets the frozen information gain control their accumulation.
309: The theorem states this conclusion on the joint event where the supplied
310: confidence and certificates hold.
311: 
312: \begin{theorem}[Estimator- and solver-agnostic confidence transport]
313: \label{thm:transported-ucb}
314: Under the protocol above with $\lambda>0$ and $\sigma>0$, suppose
315: \Cref{asm:abstract-transport} holds, the score obeys
316: \eqref{eq:transported-score-new}--\eqref{eq:approx-score-oracle-new}, and
317: $\|\bq_t(a)\|_2\le G$.  On the joint confidence and certificate event, the
318: instantaneous regret satisfies
319: \begin{equation}\label{eq:instantaneous-transport-new}
320:  \operatorname{reg}_t\le
321:  \beta_t\!\left[1+\alpha_t e^{\bar D_t}
322:  \sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}\right]\bar s_t(a_t)
323:  +2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t.
324: \end{equation}
325: Consequently,
326: \begin{align}
327: R_T
328: &\le
329: \sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)\gamma_T
330: \sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2
331: \left[1+\alpha_t e^{\bar D_t}
332: \sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}\right]^2}
333: \nonumber\\[-1mm]
334: &\quad+2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.\label{eq:sharp-transport-regret-new}
335: \end{align}
336: In particular, the simpler bound
337: \begin{align}
338: R_T
339: &\le2\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)\gamma_T
340: \sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t^2\beta_t^2e^{2\bar D_t}
341: \frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}
342: \nonumber\\[-1mm]
343: &\quad+2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t
344: \label{eq:simple-transport-regret-new}
345: \end{align}
346: holds.  The bias envelope enters twice and the approximate-oracle error enters
347: once.  If the confidence event has probability at least $1-\delta$ and the
348: joint certificate event has probability at least $1-\delta_{\rm cert}$, these
349: bounds hold with probability at least $1-\delta-\delta_{\rm cert}$.
350: \end{theorem}
351: 
352: \paragraph{Reading the bound.}
353: The instantaneous bound has a statistical radius $\beta_t$, a frozen width
354: $\bar s_t(a_t)$, and a factor accounting for transport and computation.
355: The exponential $e^{\bar D_t}$ reflects two comparisons: a factor
356: $e^{\bar D_t/2}$ makes the current-width score optimistic, and another
357: compares the selected current width back to the frozen width for the regret
358: proof.  The ratio $\kappa_{+,t}/\kappa_{-,t}$ accounts for operator distortion,
359: and $\alpha_t$ accounts for excess width from the solver.  The additive terms
360: charge current bias and approximate score maximization.
361: 
362: Validity does not ensure that this bound is informative.  A large path
363: envelope, a weak lower operator bound, a loose solver width, or persistent
364: bias can make it vacuous.  In particular, an upper operator comparison alone
365: can support the outward comparison but cannot supply the return comparison
366: used by the displayed regret bound.
367: 
368: \paragraph{Why keep direct reference scoring as a comparator?}
369: Once a reference-confidence band is available, the learner can score actions
370: with its reference widths directly.  The next proposition states that
371: policy's guarantee on its own selected history.  It provides a baseline for
372: understanding the additional factors required by transport.
373: 
374: \begin{proposition}[Frozen-width UCB on its own trajectory]
375: \label{prop:frozen-width-ucb}
376: Keep the timing, measurability, bounded-query, and frozen-update assumptions
377: above, and assume \eqref{eq:abstract-confidence-new} along the trajectory of
378: the policy that uses
379: \[
380:  U_t^{\rm fr}(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a).
381: \]
382: Assume its score supremum is finite and measurable and its pre-reward
383: measurable selector satisfies
384: $U_t^{\rm fr}(a_t)\ge\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t^{\rm fr}(a)-\xi_t$.
385: On the reference-confidence event,
386: \begin{align}
387:  \operatorname{reg}_t
388:  &\le 2\beta_t\bar s_t(a_t)+2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t,\nonumber\\
389:  R_T
390:  &\le 2\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)
391:  \gamma_T\sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2}
392:  +2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.
393:  \label{eq:frozen-width-regret}
394: \end{align}
395: All quantities are evaluated on this policy's own selected history.  No path,
396: current-metric, or operator certificate is needed for this score.  If its
397: reference-confidence event has probability at least $1-\delta$, so does this
398: guarantee.
399: \end{proposition}
